meta.title: Drill Library
meta.subtitle: Practice material, small-sided games and teaching clips

items.title: 1v1 Around the Chair
items.summary: Offense starts by circling a chair, so the rep begins with the defender already in a live stance. Simple way to open practice with a contested first step.
items.notes: From your doc — no clip attached.

items.title: 1v2 — Back to Basket, First to Touch the Cone
items.summary: Two defenders, one attacker with his back to the basket. Whoever touches the cone first earns the advantage, so the read happens before the catch.
items.notes: From your doc — no clip attached.

items.title: Line Foot 1v1
items.summary: The defender may not move his foot until the attacker leaves. Builds a genuine closing-distance problem instead of a static stance.
items.notes: From your doc — no clip attached.

items.title: Chameleon 1v1 — Three Starting Conditions
items.summary: One game, three reads depending on where it starts: (a) close to the rim with the back to the basket, (b) close to the rim off the shoulder — can also start from the dribble with a hand down, (c) far from the rim playing advantage-or-clock.
items.notes: X link — caption could not be pulled; described from your notes.

items.title: Feel Hand 1v1 — Close the Gap, Attack the Rib Cage
items.summary: Starts tight with the defender holding the advantage. The attacker veers into the defender on the drive, which improves both the driving angle and the finishing angle.
items.notes: Your framing is the intel/feel hand; the source frames it as closing the gap into the rib cage. Same rep, two coaching cues.

items.title: Mikan Drill With a Partner
items.summary: Mikan with a live second player added, so the touch work happens under interference instead of unopposed.

items.title: 1v1 Off a Chair Jump
items.summary: Finishing in a confined space where the player has to invent the solution. Constrained area plus live defense is what produces the unexpected finishes.

items.title: 1v1 From a Disadvantage — Finishing
items.summary: Offense starts behind, so every finish is contested from a trailing position. Sold as a defensive-effort drill as much as a finishing one.

items.title: Nuisance Race 1v1 — Puzzle Per Rep
items.summary: Each rep is a small problem to solve, and the rules change to steer the focus: off hand only, must initiate contact before the finish, finish on the opposite side from where you started, or vary the starting position. Players can also be told to strip or block each other.
items.notes: The source calls this his go-to offseason warm-up. The constraint list is the valuable part.

items.title: Floater 1v1 — Defender Touches the Baseline
items.summary: Offense starts on either wing with the ball, defense starts on the smiley. Defense moves first and touches the baseline; offense responds and must attack middle toward the free-throw line, finishing with an open-hand floater off either foot or off two. Defense contests.
items.notes: You flagged this as good floater work — the source built the whole rule set around exactly that.

items.title: Make It Take It 1v1
items.summary: Fast-paced finishing game — scorer keeps the ball, so runs of possession go to whoever is finishing.

items.title: Take the Ball — Finishing Warm-Up
items.summary: Both players stand close to the basket, one holding the ball. The other works to take it; whoever wins it finishes, the loser plays defense. Switch sides and holder every rep, one point per make, live offensive rebound, first to five.
items.notes: You noted it also works from the dribble and with two players a side.

items.title: Rock, Paper, Scissors Finishing
items.summary: Two players face each other side-on to the basket in the midrange, with a third holding a ball slightly behind. They play rock-paper-scissors; the winner takes the ball and attacks with a two-dribble maximum.

items.title: Transition 1v1 — Defender Picks the Angle
items.summary: The offensive player gets an advantage turning the corner while the defender chooses an angle that gives him a chance at a stop. Difficulty is tuned by adjusting the starting gap.

items.title: Shoulder Ball 1v1 — Reaction Start
items.summary: Reaction-based start built around agility and split-second decisions rather than a scripted first move.

items.title: Tag With a Flag in the Shorts
items.summary: Tag game where a cloth tucked into the shorts is the target. Gets change of direction and evasion in before anyone touches a ball.
items.notes: X link — caption could not be pulled; described from your notes.

items.title: Ball Control Warm-Up — Goalkeeper Variation
items.summary: Ball-control warm-up borrowed from goalkeeper training. Handling under unfamiliar demands rather than standard stationary dribbling.

items.summary: Players run around a cone (or around the coach) to start the possession, which scrambles the matchup and creates a live special-situation start.

items.title: Stairs for Teaching Footwork
items.summary: Uses a set of stairs as the constraint for teaching footwork patterns — the step height forces the sequencing you want.

items.title: Euro Step — Single-Leg Stability
items.summary: Balance work isolating each leg separately so the player can absorb and redirect on either foot in a live scoring situation.

items.title: Cone Slides for a Low Dribble
items.summary: Cone slides force the low body position most players can't reach on their own. One rep under the cone teaches the shoulder drop that years of unconstrained reps won't.
items.notes: Strong argument in the caption for constraint over instruction.

items.title: Ball Control Against Contact
items.summary: Handling drill built to beat defenders who hand check or play physical. Also works as a 1v1 start.
items.notes: Demoed with Tyrese Maxey.

items.title: Punch — Breakdown

items.summary: Footwork and coordination drill with a lot of moving pieces at once. Explicitly flagged by the source as not for beginners.

items.title: Red Zone Defense — Wall-Ups and Verticals
items.summary: LSU practicing defense without fouling: wall-ups and verticality, drilled on day one of practice so the habit is set before the season.
items.notes: Good fit for your red-zone framing — contest hard without reaching.

items.title: Aggressiveness Drills

items.title: Advantage or Clock — With the Nudge
items.summary: The core advantage-or-clock game with the nudge used to set the starting advantage. In 2v2 add the principle of filling one pass away from the ball, and advance if you didn't get the pass.
items.notes: Caption blocked — described from your notes. This is your base game; several others are variations of it.

items.title: Hot Potato
items.summary: In 2v2 add an attacker in a reaction position. Can start from a guard spot with a player ready weak-side — if he closes too far and doesn't space, he runs.
items.notes: Facebook caption could not be pulled — described from your notes.

items.title: 1v1 With One in the Middle

items.title: Body Fakes 1v1 — Mastering the Hesi
items.summary: Two parts: hesitation without the dribble, then hesitation with a dribble progression. Built to keep defenders guessing rather than to drill a fixed move.

items.title: 1v1 — Five Situations

items.title: High Five — Off-Ball Movement
items.summary: Off-ball movement game where help is only legal after the pass. In 2v2 add a help defender who is allowed to arrive.

items.title: 2v1 From Varied Starts
items.summary: 2v1 launched from several different starting positions so the read changes each rep.

items.title: 1v1 — Touch the Line
items.summary: A line touch sets the starting advantage. Framed around the idea that a made layup can still be a defensive win if the contest was right.
items.notes: Useful cue for players who judge defense only by whether the shot went in.

items.title: Villanova 1v1 — Must Finish Off Two Feet
items.summary: 1v1 variation with a hard constraint: every finish must come off a two-foot stop. Named Villanova by the source for exactly that scoring-off-two habit.

items.title: Handoff 1v1 to 2v1
items.summary: Two teams line up on one wing. Defense starts with the ball and hands it off so offense attacks middle, into a 2v1 with a wing and a corner player. The lone defender chooses: stop the ball, take away the wing, or take away the corner. Offense scores points for baskets, defense for stops. Roughly 2:30 per side, then switch offense/defense and switch sides of the court.
items.notes: The source builds up to it: first handoff 1v1 alone for cutting the angle and finishes, then the same offensive setup with a coach on dummy D to teach the reads, jump stops, correct-hand passing and cut timing.

items.title: 1v1 Lateral Slides, Defender Facing the Basket
items.summary: Defensive-side player development — the defender starts facing the basket and has to reorient while sliding. The source treats this side of the ball as a genuine separator.

items.title: Start Leaning on the Defender, Hands in the Shoulder Pocket
items.summary: The rep starts from contact. Getting the feet behind you and using that to create an explosive first step and separation is what makes attacking off the dribble easier.

items.title: 1v1 for Off-Ball Movement — Cut or Backdoor
items.summary: Reading the moment to cut: front cut or backdoor. Offense stays calm and cuts to the rim when the defender touches the cone; the defense is trying to touch and recover.
items.notes: You rated this one highly for off-ball work. Source caption is in Spanish.

items.title: 4v4 — Help the Helper
items.summary: Man-to-man rotation game. Also teaches the offensive side of a collapsed defense — what's open once help commits. The source teaches man-to-man exclusively on the argument that youth players need to think as they play.
items.notes: Your doc also lists this clip under shooting fixes (knees too far forward/back) — that's a mislink, this clip is about defense.

items.title: Three-Point Line as the Backdoor Trigger
items.summary: Iowa uses the three-point line itself as the cue for backdoor cuts — a positional trigger players can read without a call.
items.notes: Good one to send players before teaching the concept live.

items.title: Feel Hand — Shoulder Bumps vs Forearm
items.summary: Two different tools for two different jobs: shoulder bumps to create contact and buy extra space, the forearm to keep a defender off your inside hip. Know what you're trying to accomplish, then pick the technique — and don't shy away from contact when it's needed.

items.title: Guarding a Big in the Post

items.title: Hip Swivel / Chair Shooting Without Legs

items.title: Crossover — Shifting Defensive Balance
items.summary: Using footwork to tip the defender's balance is what makes beating him easier — the crossover finishes a job the feet already started.

items.title: Floater
items.summary: Floater as the fix for players who keep getting layups blocked.

items.title: Closeout — Take Away the Three
items.summary: The intent of this closeout style is to take away the three and stop the shooter from shooting at all. If he does shoot, be in position for a strong contest. The perfect closeout takes away the three and still stays in front once the ball goes to the floor.

items.title: Closeouts — Sprint and Stop, Don't Chop
items.summary: Direct argument against chopping the feet on a closeout. Strides shorten as you get closer, but that isn't chopping — in game clips every player sprints and stops. Chopping feet is what gets players burned.
items.notes: Worth watching alongside the howtomakethenba closeout clips — they agree on intent, this one is sharper on the footwork.

items.summary: Closeout defense as the most misunderstood part of defending. Elite defensive teams have players who sprint into the closeout to force a hard contest or put the ball on the floor. Jrue Holiday and Derrick White are the reference examples.
